pending_articles.title: "The Rose Garden Is a Cemetery": Spatial Dissonance and Divergent Public Experiences of an Indigenous Augmented Reality Tour
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.19641v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Community-authored augmented reality (AR) can contest dominant heritage narratives by juxtaposing stories with physical surroundings. We examine the Th\'amien Ohlone AR Tour, developed with members of the Ohlone Native American community at Mission Santa Clara and Santa Clara University. Combining paired pre/post surveys from 57 participants with collaborative thematic analysis, we compare reception among Ohlone community members, university affiliates, and Mission visitors. Spatial dissonance captures felt tensions when AR challenged familiar campus readings or when surroundings conflicted with Ohlone histories the AR affirmed, such as a garden's significance as a burial ground. Cultural frames shaped interpretation; contemporary people and relationships made Ohlone continuance tangible. Participants appreciated the tour and called for permanent physical acknowledgment. We propose staging reflective encounters, clarifying community-authored meanings, and using AR to prototype public acknowledgment and support community-directed advocacy. These findings foreground relationships to land and place, informed by Indigenous scholarship, in designing and evaluating AR.
pending_articles.author: Grace Fujii, Vittorio Murtas, Sarah Sallee, Isabella 'Amne Gomez, Lauren Baines, Danielle Heitmuller, Amy Lueck, Kai Lukoff

pending_articles.title: Beyond Initial Creation: Two Decades of Community-based Chart Revisions from Wikimedia Commons
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.19337v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Open online communities like Wikipedia offer a rich space for understanding the organic evolution of public-facing artifacts, but little is known about how these communities collectively edit chart images. We investigate the phenomenon of "community editing" of visualizations by exploring chart revision patterns on Wikimedia Commons. We introduce a novel dataset of 7,786 longitudinal chart revisions across 1,664 images, labeled with edit categories using an LLM pipeline. Initial data analysis uncovered several novel findings. Multi-contributor revision is associated with more edits to mark styling and text content compared to single-contributor revision. Temporally, mark and text edits occur in more "bursty" cadences than data edits. In addition, while SVG charts attract more unique contributors and revisions than raster charts, their edit histories involve more tightly scoped and less diverse changes. This dataset enables a wide range of analyses of chart change over time.
pending_articles.author: Jasmine Y. Shih, Chase Stokes, Melanie Tory, Marti Hearst

pending_articles.title: Moving Beyond the Flat Screen: Opportunities and Challenges of Extended Reality for Studying Human Brain and Behavior
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.19199v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Much of what we know about human perception and cognition comes from austere experimental settings: static stimuli presented to sedentary observers on flat monitors, complex responses reduced to simple button presses, and brain activity recorded from immobilized heads using EEG or fMRI. These highly controlled paradigms have provided remarkable insights, but capture a small and often unusual slice of behavior, raising questions about how well the findings generalize to the real world. Extended reality (XR), spanning both immersive virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) that overlays digital content on the real world, offers a way beyond these constraints, supporting controlled, reproducible experiments in which participants actively engage with three-dimensional tasks. Drawing on a growing body of VR and AR studies of attention, memory, and language -- our own and others', some involving EEG -- we outline what XR makes newly possible for cognitive neuroscience and reflect on the practical and conceptual obstacles that remain. The opportunities are substantial, but realizing them requires solving practical problems of hardware, timing, and measurement, and being realistic about what a virtual or augmented world can and cannot stand in for.
pending_articles.author: Tom Bullock, Radha Kumaran, You-Jin Kim, Emily Machniak, Tobias H\"ollerer, Barry Giesbrecht

pending_articles.title: Understanding Goalball Training Across Roles and Team Contexts: Practices, Perceptions, Challenges, and Technological Opportunities
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.19160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Goalball is a team sport for visually impaired athletes, played by throwing and blocking a ball while wearing eyeshades. However, existing studies provide limited guidance on which everyday training difficulties technology should address for players and coaches across team contexts. We conducted semi-structured interviews and focus groups with 18 players and 12 coaches from seven South Korean teams spanning youth, second-division, first-division, and national-team contexts. Using qualitative coding and matrix-based analysis, we describe current training practices, participants' views of these methods, the challenges they encounter, and their technological support needs. Drawing on the relationships among these four areas, we discuss implications for the design and evaluation of future support technologies that fit everyday goalball training across roles and team contexts.
pending_articles.author: Gyeongdeok Kim, Junhyuk Jang, Donghyeon Kim, Billy Park, Gunhyuk Park

pending_articles.title: Iterative Design and Evaluation of a VR Nursing Training System: Insights from Clinicians and Student Learners
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2610.19152v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents the iterative design and evaluation of a virtual reality (VR) nursing training system developed in collaboration with nursing education specialists to enhance procedural skill acquisition, clinical decision-making, and critical thinking among pre-licensure nursing students. Two clinical scenarios, chest pain and oxygen therapy, were created to simulate acute care settings, with design refinements informed by an expert evaluation study (n=8) and further assessed through an effectiveness study involving nursing students (n=17). Results demonstrate high user acceptance, perceived usefulness, and significant post-simulation increases in learner confidence. The VR system was found to be an accessible supplemental training tool that can foster self-directed learning. Finally, we present design recommendations for developing VR simulations for nursing education, emphasizing collaboration with domain experts, accommodating diverse learning goals, and simulating complex clinical workflows.
pending_articles.author: Danhua Zhang, Cynthia Bradley, Christopher Kissell, Courtney Hutton Pospick, Seraphina Yong, Qiao Jin, Tongyu Nie, Evan Suma Rosenberg

pending_articles.title: NeuronSifter: An Agent-in-Twin for Prioritizing Central Nervous System Interventions with World Action Models
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2609.35445v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Effective central nervous system (CNS) intervention requires more than predicting biological responses: a scientific system must determine which intervention, observation, or additional evidence can improve a decision under uncertainty. However, in partially observed neuronal microenvironments, identical predicted outcomes may correspond to different exposure states, biological mechanisms, and intervention risks. We propose NeuronSifter, a decision-centric Agent-in-Twin framework, where an AI agent operates with an evolving biological digital twin rather than a fixed predictive model. NeuronSifter compiles interventions into state-conditional target-occupancy representations, propagates them through a mechanism-grounded World Action Model (WAM), and selects informative measurements based on their expected reduction in decision uncertainty. A shared probabilistic belief state couples intervention simulation, observation selection, and outcome assimilation, enabling the digital twin to continuously refine its decision-relevant representations through externally verified evidence. We evaluate NeuronSifter in Alzheimer's disease intervention scenarios using mechanistic neuronal microenvironment simulations and retrospective clinical endpoint references. The evaluation framework examines adaptive evidence acquisition, uncertainty-aware intervention planning, and robustness under model discrepancy through controlled environments and independent comparisons. NeuronSifter demonstrates how an AI system can actively identify missing evidence, refine biological hypotheses, and optimize intervention decisions under limited experimental budgets. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/NeuronSifter.
pending_articles.author: Haowei Xu, Wanyi Fu, Hongbin Han, Zhaoheng Xie

pending_articles.title: NeuronDiscover: Agent-in-Twin for Mechanistic Discovery in Neuronal Microenvironments with World Action Models
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2609.35338v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Mechanistic discovery in neuronal microenvironments requires interventions and measurements that separate competing explanations of solute transport and neuronal response. Predictive accuracy cannot settle the question: a real mechanistic change and an error in the computational twin leave the same signature in sparse observations. We formalize this twin confounding and reason over a joint mechanism--discrepancy belief, designing experiments that separate the two. NeuronDiscover is an Agent-in-Twin framework whose shared, mechanism-grounded World Action Model (WAM) couples prediction, intervention proposals, and observation design; independently adjudicated outcomes revise a scoped Mechanism--Intervention--Observation--Outcome (MIOY) graph, whose supported relations compile into executable programs carrying discrepancy-adjusted acceptance bounds. We evaluate on simulated brain-fluid tracer-transport worlds adjudicated by an independently frozen finer-mesh reference solver, and on donor-disjoint public current-clamp recordings of cortical neurons. Counting only relations that reach a certified terminal status, and scoring abstentions as unresolved for every method, at a matched budget of 16 experiments over 32 source units NeuronDiscover resolves 4.0 relations per assigned world against 3.4 for the strongest baseline and 3.2 without graph revision, at 5% false support and 82% scope accuracy. Joint mechanism--discrepancy acquisition resolves 3.8 relations versus 2.9 for plug-in expected information gain; discrepancy-adjusted verification lowers accepted-program failure from 15% to 9% at 60% acceptance coverage; and transfer to the recordings yields 1.94 versus 1.53 relations per assigned world. Correctness is adjudicated within declared model worlds and archival recordings.
pending_articles.author: Haowei Xu, Wanyi Fu, Hongbin Han, Zhaoheng Xie

pending_articles.title: Position: Hippocampal Explicit Memory Is the Cornerstone for AGI
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2606.11245v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, raising expectations for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). This position paper argues that integrating explicit memory is the cornerstone for advancing LLMs toward AGI. The key reason is that the underlying learning mechanism of LLMs is highly analogous to human implicit memory. However, higher-order cognitive functions necessary for AGI, such as long-term strategic planning, metacognition, and symbolic reasoning, heavily rely on hippocampal explicit memory and cannot arise solely from implicit statistical learning. Drawing on findings from neuroscience, I advance this perspective and complement it with computational requirements for artificial explicit memory systems, hoping to foster further research and lay the groundwork for explicit memory integration.
pending_articles.author: Sangjun Park

pending_articles.title: Simulation Based Inference of a Simple Neural Network Structure
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2604.18599v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Neurophysiologists are nowadays able to record from a large number of extracellular electrodes and to extract, from the raw data, the sequences of action potentials or spikes generated by many neurons. Unfortunately these ''many neurons'' still represent only a tiny fraction of the neuronal population that constitutes the network. Using association statistics such as the estimation of the cross-correlation functions, they are trying to infer the structure of the network formed by the recorded neurons. But this inference is compromised by the tremendous under-sampling of the neuronal population. We propose to focus instead on simple spike train statistics, like the empirical spikes frequency, or the interspike interval distribution. Their sampling distributions can be estimated by simulations, and, given a few observed spike train statistics, they provide enough information to infer the structure of the underlying network. We show that, on a ''toy model'', our method gives significantly better results than the sub-network reconstruction method with regards to the inference of the connection probability of the original network.
pending_articles.author: Pierre Charitat (IRMA), S\'egolen Geffray (IRMA), Christophe Pouzat (IRMA)

pending_articles.title: State Space Models Naturally Produce Time Cell and Oscillatory Behaviors and Scale to Abstract Cognitive Functions
pending_articles.content:
arXiv:2507.13638v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A grand challenge in modern neuroscience is bridging the gap between the microscale neural circuits and cognitive functions. While extensive knowledge exists about neuronal connectivity and biophysics, how low-level phenomena give rise to abstract behaviors remains largely unresolved. Here, we propose that a mathematical framework based on State Space Models offers mathematical sufficiency and computational plausibility to generate response profiles that resemble time cells, ramping activity, and oscillatory responses. Our results suggest that such behaviors can emerge from a structured multi-timescale complex rotational basis, which enables optimized history compression and naturally generates structured temporal dynamics even prior to training, mirroring recent findings in biological circuits. Learning exploits and adapts to the pre-existing temporal basis for specific tasks. We show that the model can readily scale to abstract cognitive functions such as event counting, supporting its use as a computationally tractable framework for understanding neural activities.
pending_articles.author: Sen Lu, Xiaoyu Zhang, Mingtao Hu, Eric Yeu-Jer Lee, Soohyeon Kim, Wei D. Lu

recently_processed.title: Task-State Governance: A Virtual Machine for Verifiable and Recoverable GUI Agent Execution
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.20100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents now execute workflows across real applications, but when execution drifts, users must determine what changed, what should have remained untouched, and what can still be recovered. Plan-centric interfaces leave users supervising procedure, but users live with changes to application state. We introduce task-state governance, an interaction paradigm that represents a task as an editable contract linking desired outcomes, facts that must be preserved, and observed application state. We instantiate this paradigm in TaskVM, which projects live state into editable task controls, executes user edits as genuine interface actions, verifies outcomes through independent observation, and marks each action as reversible, compensatable, or irreversible. Across an automated contract benchmark, a controlled user study, and an open live-model exploration, the paradigm strengthened contract compliance and users' recovery control and trust, while execution outcomes were held constant. Task contracts open a design space for governable agent interfaces.
recently_processed.author: Wenkui Yang, Yiming Hao, Kai Zhou, Chengyu Pu, Yuzhe Zhang, Jie Cao, Jin Huang, Shuai Ma, Feng Tian

recently_processed.title: Scoping the Landscape of Large Language Model-based Affective Personal Informatics: Review, Reflection, Future Direction
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.20084v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Affective personal informatics (PI) involves capturing, tracking, analyzing, and reflecting on personal data to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are reshaping affective PI, yet a comprehensive survey of LLM-based affective PI systems is lacking. To bridge this gap, we systematically analyzed 45 papers published between January 2020 and June 2026 across four major computing and health databases, examining their macro trends, system taxonomies, and research methodologies. Our synthesis reveals an overreliance on multi-stage, text-centric pipelines, a predominance of active, screen-bound interactions, and a severe demographic skew toward young, university-campus-based cohorts in empirical evaluations. Based on these findings, we critically reflect on prevailing architectural and methodological shortcomings and outline actionable future directions for building end-to-end multimodal, low-burden, and inclusive affective PI systems.
recently_processed.author: Minjie Liu, Lihuan Li, Xuran Li, Flora Salim, Benjamin Tag

recently_processed.title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.19998v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough in real time via shader injection. When receiving a user's prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user's intent, analyzes the user's view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage patterns, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how ("Highlight the book."), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental or behavioral states ("Make me laugh."). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., "Make me not miss my flight") while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.
recently_processed.author: Yanni Mei, Samuel Hartenstein, Jonas Wombacher, Florian Mueller, Jan Gugenheimer

recently_processed.title: Think Once, Reflect Twice: How Feedback Shapes Human-AI Collaboration
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.19991v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports human decision-making in high-stakes domains, designing effective human-AI collaboration becomes critical. Successful collaboration requires humans to reflect on decision-making processes and adjust their strategies accordingly. Current research typically investigates interventions, such as explainable AI, that target reflection during the decision-making process (reflection-in-action). Less attention has been given to retrospective examination of decisions (reflection-on-action). This work explores reflection-on-action by studying the impact of feedback on reliance behavior and human-AI team performance. Specifically, we investigate feedback interventions targeting overrides of AI advice through a behavioral study (N=244). We find that such feedback influences reflection-on-action, while unidirectional feedback risks reducing subsequent reflection-in-action. Furthermore, we identify opposing shifts in reliance behavior that leave overall human-AI team performance unchanged but show context-dependent effects. Balanced feedback did not show these risks, preserving both concurrent and retrospective reflection, offering insights for designing for appropriate reliance on AI.
recently_processed.author: Joshua Holstein, Philipp Spitzer, Sebastian Sch\"afer, Maximilian F\"orster, Gerhard Satzger

recently_processed.title: AdaptaFace: Adversarial Assistance for Inclusive Facial Gesture Interaction
recently_processed.content:
arXiv:2610.19977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Facial gestures can enable access for people with motor impairments (PwM), yet recognizers may not reliably interpret individual facial movement patterns. Existing approaches either constrain agency by requiring predefined templates or impose repeated calibration, data collection, and computation through user-specific retraining. We present AdaptaFace, an input-level compatibility layer using bounded, proxy-dependent adversarial perturbations to translate user-compatible gestures into inputs for an unchanged facial action unit (AU)-based recognizer. Designed around six personalization principles informed by interviews with 12 PwM, AdaptaFace supports both recognition enhancement and gesture vocabulary extension. In a within-subject study with 16 participants, AdaptaFace increased task completion from 59.7% to 90.5% and reduced workload from 5.61 to 4.21. Offline validation showed strong steering with aligned perturbation generation and evaluation but weaker cross-recognizer transfer, defining the approach's boundary. These findings frame adversarial assistance as input-side accessibility mediation for personalized facial-gesture interaction.
recently_processed.author: Siyu Zhang, Yelu Gu, Xiaoyun Xu, Kirsten Cater, Oussama Metatla

recently_processed.title: A canonical neural circuit for motion direction estimation
recently_processed.content: Abundant experimental data support the view that motion detection is a canonical neural operation, common to a wide variety of species and different stages in the visual stream. However, existing motion models lack this generality, as their predictive power tends to be restricted to some specific visual phenomena, brain regions, or animal taxa. Here, we introduce a neural circuit model that only uses cells selective to cardinal directions, with elements that can be interpreted as emulating some dendritic processes, and we show how it is able to predict a wide range of visual motion data, from basic properties to hitherto unexplained phenomena, surpassing state-of-the-art models implemented as deep neural networks with millions of parameters. The direction-selective cells that our model relies on are present in the visual systems of many classes of animals, from insects to primates, and in visual pathway structures going from the retina to the cortex, suggesting that the proposed model could serve as a canonical neural circuit for estimating motion direction.
recently_processed.author: Berraquero, M., Serrano-Pedraza, I., Bertalmio, M.

recently_processed.title: From haptic exploration to object perception in 3D
recently_processed.content: Active touch determines which parts of an object are sampled and therefore which sensory information becomes available for perception. However, little is known about how the three-dimensional geometry of an object guides exploratory hand movements and how the information acquired during exploration contributes to perceptual decisions. Here, we investigated these questions in two experiments in which blindfolded participants explored 3D-printed replicas of bell-peppers while their hand movements were recorded using motion tracking. The task of participants' was to identify the reference object among two comparison objects (target & competitor). In the first experiment, objects were presented in a fixed orientation, whereas in the second, object orientation varied across presentations to disrupt the correspondence between hand configuration and object geometry. We first trained a neural network to predict the spatial distribution of touch directly from three-dimensional surface structure. The model successfully predicted touch locations on previously unseen objects, outperforming a generic spatial exploration prior in both experiments. Geometric analyses revealed that haptic saliency was associated with specific combinations of local surface curvatures rather than simply with the overall magnitude of curvature. We then examined whether the information acquired during exploration could predict subsequent recognition choices, considering global and local surface geometry and potential memory decay of acquired object representations. Models integrating global and local information across the complete exploration reliably identified the objectively correct object and correct participants' choices. In contrast, restricting the comparison to temporally proximal portions of successive explorations reduced objective recognition accuracy but increased correspondence with participants' errors. Overall, our findings suggest that haptic exploration is at least to some extent driven by object-specific geometry, but that the information acquired is not necessarily integrated optimally into perceptual decisions. Instead, memory limitations and potentially incomplete integration may constrain how sampled three-dimensional shape information contributes to recognition.
recently_processed.author: Metzger, A., Toscani, M.

recently_processed.title: Language-associated brain representations covary with disruption of selfhood under psilocybin
recently_processed.content: Language helps organise experience into an idiosyncratic, temporally extended sense of self. We therefore used fMRI to investigate whether greater similarity between participants in the activity of language-associated brain regions accompanied psilocybin-induced loss of selfhood. Participants heard music and viewed moving clouds at baseline and after 19 mg psilocybin. At each brain location and time point, we tested whether similarity increased with each pair's summed rank on the Ego Dissolution Inventory (EDI; N=43). We grouped independent components of these associations by time course and decoded each group's map with Neurosynth. Elementary visual imagery (SI; N=49) and baseline activity served as comparators. Under psilocybin, one group formed a distributed, left-lateralised frontotemporal network matching the Neurosynth language map (r=.382, spatial-null p<.001, q=.003), nearly twice the largest comparator estimate (SI: r=.208, p=.004, q=.028; baseline: r<.12). In exploratory analyses, resting-state connectivity of this network decreased with posterior visual cortex and increased with thalamic and frontal regions. Participants with higher EDI scores showed larger changes (Spearman's rho=.455, Bonferroni-adjusted p=.048; SI: rho=.008), most strongly for items describing loss of ego or identity (rho=.43 to .51). We propose that language-associated systems incorporate each person's semantic and autobiographical context into experience, and that disrupting them contributes to loss of ego and identity.
recently_processed.author: Cooper, G., Stoliker, D., Astl Delgado, S. V., Blackburne, G., Novelli, L., Green, D. W., Razi, A., Das, R. K., Skipper, J. I.

recently_processed.title: Apoptosis at the optic fissure shapes transient retinal myeloid states
recently_processed.content: Microglia and CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs) originate from yolk sac erythromyeloid progenitors, yet the process that mediates their colonization of the mammalian eye and the developmental cues that promote their diversification remain unclear. Here, we identify the optic fissure as the primary entry site for myeloid cells into the embryonic mouse retina. This entry is spatially and temporally coupled with a localized wave of cell death. This apoptotic niche contains colonizing myeloid cells in a transient CD206+ state, and apoptotic burden directly correlates with CD206 expression across development. We find that disrupting apoptotic recognition pathways, specifically Cx3cr1 and Itgam, promotes enrichment of CD206+ cells; likewise, increasing cell death via genetic loss of Atoh7 results in elevated CD206+ population, indicating that impaired clearance and increased death converge on a common outcome within a constrained developmental window. Both CD206+ and CD206- subsets contribute to phagocytosis during optic fissure closure, indicating that CD206 expression does not mark a specialized phagocytic subset. Intriguingly, unlike parenchymal microglia, CD206+ cells are selectively spared from pharmacological CSF1R inhibition, revealing distinct survival requirements within the fissure niche. Together, these findings indicate that localized apoptotic niches encountered during myeloid cell entry influence the initial states and properties of CNS-resident myeloid cells.
recently_processed.author: Ghena, N., Warner, W. S., Landaverde Rodriguez, Y., Schwakopf, J., Roberts, J. M., Vetter, M. L.

recently_processed.title: Rescuing anxiety by targeting the neuronal-astrocytic iron signaling axis in male mice
